# Spring Boot readiness and graceful shutdown in a container

A container that serves requests after startup can still lose work when it is
replaced. This example uses the workshop’s Spring Boot quote service to show
when an instance reports readiness and what happens to a request already in
progress when Docker asks its JVM to stop.

The walkthrough starts an eight-second quote request, sends `SIGTERM` to the
Java process through `docker stop`, and checks that the response completes
before the container exits. This focused example does not cover every aspect of
running Java in containers. See the
[all-in-one example](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md) for a more holistic
treatment of image construction, limits, security, and diagnostics.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the readiness endpoint and the graceful shutdown settings;
- verify that the quote service reports readiness before receiving work;
- observe an in-flight request finish after the JVM receives `SIGTERM`; and
- explain why the platform’s termination limit must allow enough time for the
  application to finish its expected requests.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- Docker with a running Linux container engine.

- `curl`, used to request readiness and a slow quote from the host.

## The artefacts to inspect

This module reuses the quote service, database, and `/quote/random` endpoint
from the other Spring Boot examples. The following three files contain the
changes needed for the lifecycle demonstration.

`SlowQuoteController.java` adds `/quote/slow`. It waits before returning a
quote, giving us a request that is still in progress when shutdown begins. The
delay is for this demonstration, not a production API.

```java
package demo.quote;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import org.springframework.web.server.ResponseStatusException;

import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/quote")
public class SlowQuoteController {

    private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(SlowQuoteController.class);

    private final QuoteService service;

    public SlowQuoteController(final QuoteService service) {
        this.service = requireNonNull(service, "The quote service cannot be null");
    }

    @GetMapping("/slow")
    public ResponseEntity<Quote> slow(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "8") final int seconds) {
        if (seconds < 0 || seconds > 30) {
            return ResponseEntity.badRequest().build();
        }

        LOGGER.info("Slow quote request started; waiting {} seconds", seconds);
        try {
            Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L);
        } catch (final InterruptedException _) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).build();
        }

        LOGGER.info("Slow quote request completed");
        return service.random()
                .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
                .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
}
```

`application.yml` enables the Actuator readiness endpoint and makes graceful
shutdown explicit. It allows up to 15 seconds per shutdown phase for requests
already in progress to finish.

```yaml
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 15s
  datasource:
    hikari:
      jdbc-url: 'jdbc:h2:mem:demo;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;MODE=MYSQL'
      username: 'demo'
      password: 'Java Containers Demo 2026'
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: none

server:
  shutdown: graceful

management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
```

The Dockerfile copies the executable JAR. Its `HEALTHCHECK` asks Spring Boot’s
readiness endpoint whether the application can receive traffic; Docker records
the result as the container’s health status. The image already includes `curl`,
so the check adds no package, but it runs a small process on every probe. The
check uses the container’s loopback interface; it does not depend on the
published host port.

Docker checks every five seconds and allows each check three seconds to finish.
During the first 30 seconds, failures do not count towards the three consecutive
failures needed to report `unhealthy` until a check succeeds. That success can
report `healthy` immediately, after which later failures count even within the
30 seconds. This period does not delay the first check. `curl --fail` turns an
HTTP error or failed connection into a failed check, while
`--silent --output /dev/null` discards the response. Docker records the health
status but does not restart the container or control traffic routing on its own.

Java starts directly as the container’s main process, so it receives the
termination signal sent by `docker stop`.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/application-lifecycle-spring-boot-*.jar"
COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

EXPOSE 8080

# The Oracle JDK image includes curl. Docker reports this container as healthy
# when Spring Boot says it is ready to receive traffic.
HEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --timeout=3s --start-period=30s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl --fail --silent --output "/dev/null" "http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator/health/readiness" || exit 1

# Exec form keeps Java as PID 1 so docker stop delivers SIGTERM to the JVM.
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

## Build the application

Run the commands from this example directory. Maven produces
`target/application-lifecycle-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar`, which the image packages
unchanged.

1. Build and test the quote service.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── application-lifecycle-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── application-lifecycle-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the packaged application

   This starts the JAR outside a container. A successful endpoint response
   establishes that the application artefact works before its runtime layout is
   changed by container packaging.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/application-lifecycle-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Print the application readiness state.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/actuator/health/readiness' | jq
   ```

   The application readiness state

   ```json
   {
     "status": "UP"
   }
   ```

   Fetch a random quote. A JSON response confirms that the packaged service is
   running and can serve its endpoint.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Henry Ford",
     "id": 72,
     "quote": "Failure is simply the opportunity to begin again, this time more intelligently."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

1. Build the container image. The Java process runs as the container’s main
   process, so it receives the container’s termination signal.

   With Docker, build and load the image using the following command.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'demo:application-lifecycle-spring-boot' \
     --load \
     .
   ```

   With Podman, specify the Docker image format so the image retains the
   Dockerfile’s `HEALTHCHECK`. The later commands use that health check to
   inspect the container’s readiness status.

   ```shell
   podman build \
     --format docker \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'demo:application-lifecycle-spring-boot' \
     .
   ```

   Build time depends on the host, registry access, and cached layers.

2. Start the container. Docker begins running the image's `HEALTHCHECK` against
   Spring Boot’s readiness endpoint. Port `8080` is bound only to the host’s
   loopback interface.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --detach \
     --name 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot' \
     --publish '8080:8080' \
     'demo:application-lifecycle-spring-boot'
   ```

3. Check the image format and the container’s readiness status. Podman must
   build this image in Docker format to retain the Dockerfile’s `HEALTHCHECK`.
   First, inspect the image’s manifest type. The expected value is
   `application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json`.

   ```shell
   podman image inspect localhost/demo:application-lifecycle-spring-boot \
     --format '{{.ManifestType}}'
   ```

   The image manifest type.

   ```
   application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json
   ```

   Then inspect the running container’s health status. The Dockerfile’s health
   check queries Spring Boot’s readiness endpoint. Once that check succeeds, the
   status is `healthy`; if it still says `starting`, repeat the command after a
   few seconds. The status makes readiness observable but does not control
   traffic routing by itself.

   ```shell
   docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot'
   ```

   The container’s current health status

   ```
   starting
   ```

   Wait for the container to turn healthy.

   ```shell
   until [ "$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot')" = 'healthy' ]; do sleep 1; done
   ```

4. Start an eight-second request in the background and save its output and
  process ID. The following steps wait for the application to log that it has
  started the request, then stop the container while the request is expected to
  be in progress.

  `docker stop --time 15` sends `SIGTERM` and allows up to 15 seconds for the
  container to exit before forcing it to stop. This gives Spring Boot time to
  complete the request during graceful shutdown.

   ```shell
   # Run a slow request that will take about 8 seconds to complete in the back
   # ground
   curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 20 \
     'http://localhost:8080/quote/slow?seconds=8' \
     > './target/slow-quote.json' 2> './target/slow-quote.err' &

   # Save the request PID for later use.
   request_pid=$!

   # Wait until the application logs 'Slow quote request started' before
   # stopping the container. This confirms that the request began, although the
   # log message alone does not prove it is still in progress.
   until docker logs 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot' 2>&1 \
     | grep -q 'Slow quote request started'; do sleep 1; done

   # Ask Docker to stop the container. Docker waits for the container to exit
   # before this command returns.
   docker stop --time 15 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot'

   # After the container has stopped, check whether the background request
   # succeeded.
   if ! wait "${request_pid}"; then
     cat './target/slow-quote.err' >&2
     exit 1
   fi
   ```

   Print the quote response from the slow request.

   ```shell
   jq . './target/slow-quote.json'
   ```

   The random quote that was fetched through the slow request.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Mark Twain",
     "id": 129,
     "quote": "To succeed in life, you need two things: ignorance and confidence."
   }
   ```

   Inspect the last 10 log lines for the slow request starting, completing,
   and Spring Boot shutting down gracefully.

   ```shell
   docker logs --tail 10 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot' 2>&1
   ```

   The last 10 lines from the container logs.

   ```
   2077-04-27T11:34:56.789Z  INFO 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-1] o.a.c.c.C.[Tomcat].[localhost].[/]       : Initializing Spring DispatcherServlet 'dispatcherServlet'
   2077-04-27T11:34:56.789Z  INFO 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-1] o.s.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet        : Initializing Servlet 'dispatcherServlet'
   2077-04-27T11:34:56.790Z  INFO 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-1] o.s.web.servlet.DispatcherServlet        : Completed initialization in 1 ms
   2077-04-27T11:34:56.947Z  INFO 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-2] demo.quote.SlowQuoteController           : Slow quote request started; waiting 8 seconds
   2077-04-27T11:34:57.039Z  INFO 1 --- [ionShutdownHook] o.s.boot.tomcat.GracefulShutdown         : Commencing graceful shutdown. Waiting for active requests to complete
   2077-04-27T11:35:04.948Z  INFO 1 --- [nio-8080-exec-2] demo.quote.SlowQuoteController           : Slow quote request completed
   2077-04-27T11:35:05.107Z  INFO 1 --- [tomcat-shutdown] o.s.boot.tomcat.GracefulShutdown         : Graceful shutdown complete
   2077-04-27T11:35:05.110Z  INFO 1 --- [ionShutdownHook] j.LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean : Closing JPA EntityManagerFactory for persistence unit 'default'
   2077-04-27T11:35:05.112Z  INFO 1 --- [ionShutdownHook] com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource       : HikariPool-1 - Shutdown initiated...
   2077-04-27T11:35:05.113Z  INFO 1 --- [ionShutdownHook] com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource       : HikariPool-1 - Shutdown completed.
   ```

5. Remove the stopped container. The
   [verification script](./containers/verify-lifecycle.sh) remains available for
   repeating the same check automatically, but the commands above show each
   lifecycle step directly.

   ```shell
   docker rm 'application-lifecycle-spring-boot'
   ```

Docker’s health status makes readiness observable, but Docker does not route
traffic based on it by itself; an orchestrator or other traffic manager must be
configured to use it. During a rolling deployment, that manager should stop
sending new requests to an instance being replaced. The local check proves that
an established request can finish after `SIGTERM`; it does not prove that a
cluster has stopped routing new requests before shutdown or that every workload
finishes within 15 seconds. A shorter Docker stop timeout can still force
`SIGKILL` before Spring Boot finishes its own graceful shutdown period.

## References

- [Spring Boot application availability](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/features/spring-application.html#features.spring-application.application-availability)
- [Spring Boot graceful shutdown](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/web/graceful-shutdown.html)
- [Dockerfile `HEALTHCHECK`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/#healthcheck)
- [Docker container stop](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/stop/)

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- The Docker `HEALTHCHECK` records Spring Boot readiness as container health; a
  traffic manager must actually use readiness to control routing.
- An exec-form Java entrypoint lets the JVM receive `SIGTERM`. Spring Boot’s
  graceful shutdown then allows an established HTTP request to finish.
- Both the application’s shutdown phase and the container platform’s termination
  limit must be long enough for the work being protected.
- This example demonstrates one HTTP request under Docker. A deployment still
  needs routing coordination and tests with its own workload.
